entries.text:
They walk you up in the cold, and you drag your heels and keep your head turning. There are cloaks all round you, six or perhaps more in the dark. A rail runs along the gate-top walk, and a bar sits across the outside of the ledger-house door. At the threshold you plant your heels and say it flat and loud enough to carry through the planks: you'll hear the Foreman's terms, but you will see Tessa alive and whole with your own eyes before you say a word.

The door opens. Lamplight and the smell of beeswax and burnt paper roll out. The Foreman is behind his desk, pale and neat, with a fresh bandage under the apron and the scorched ledger sitting beside the lamp inside a locked iron-bound chest, its lid open a hand's breadth. He studies you the way a clerk studies a bad sum. Then he nods to the stove.

Tessa sits there on a stool with a needle in her fingers and a roll of linen at her feet. A dark bruise rides her temple under the bandage, and her wrists are free. She looks up at you and her face goes loose with relief, then tight again. "I'm whole, Kor," she says in Common, for the room. "He hasn't touched me. He needs the needle." Her eyes say the rest.

The Foreman lets you have that. He gestures for you to sit on the floor with your back to the table, and you talk. He is patient, and he is wearier than he was, and he does not like being asked questions. But you ask them, and he answers one in three. What the term would be if you refused. Why the captain's number went up. Whether the mountain would last another winter if the Tin Row was gone. He admits the Stones fine, and he admits it was not the whole of the sum, and he says "a debtor who sees the bottom of his debt stops working," in the voice of a man explaining a law of nature. The lamp burns lower. The cloaks along the wall shift and yawn. It is a cold hour, the hour before dawn, and the Foreman is a man who has not slept in a day and a half.

Once, while he rummages for a seal, Tessa bends over the needle and whispers in Draconic, so softly it could be thread against linen. "Brun came to me on the stair. He'll open the wash-house drain when the dawn bell rings, if we're here to use it. After that he's out of tricks."

Now it is a quarter past five. The window shutters have gone from black to charcoal. The Foreman has just picked up his pen to write your terms once more, and outside, faint and far, you hear a single iron voice begin to toll.

The dawn bell.

You are at 1 hit point, wired at wrist and ankle to the leg of a table. The guards are at the walls, and Tessa is on her stool beside the stove, with the needle in her hand. What does Korvash do?

When he was young, hobgoblins of the Iron Tallies warband, led by a tin-masked captain named Gorrak Vael (who notches a rod for every raid), overran his village. His father Dargan held the narrow Goat's Throat pass, losing a hand and then his life, so the herd and the children could flee; Korvash swore to him, with his blood on his hands, to protect the weak. His younger sister Tessa was lost in the raid and her fate is UNKNOWN: he never saw her fall and has never stopped wondering, so she must not be confirmed alive or dead unless discovered in play. The survivors fled to Harrowmere, where his aunt Veshra raised him and still sends word by travelers. The clan built a cairn at the Goat's Throat, which he has never had the heart to revisit. His shame at being too young to stand beside his father is why he is loud and makes sure everyone knows he is standing. He carries his father's second-best greataxe with Dargan's ember-red scale-sash tied to the haft. Hook for the opening: just after the bullies flee, a frightened young herder or a traveler brings him word, perhaps carried from Aunt Veshra, that a hobgoblin warband bearing a tin-masked captain and a notched rod has been seen again, or that something connected to the Goat's Throat has turned up. This pulls him toward an oath-bound choice: someone weak is in immediate danger, he promises to help, and keeping that word will lead him back toward the mountains and the questions about Tessa. entries.text:
They walk you up slow, and you drag your feet and let them think it is the weakness it half is. Your eyes work the whole way.

Six grey cloaks, the sergeant at the head, spears reversed to the butt as if you might still bolt. The gate-top walk is a ledge of black slate no wider than a cart, with the east side falling a hundred feet to the yard and a low wall along it. The west side is the ledger-house, and its two windows are shuttered with iron straps. The door is oak, barred from outside on two iron brackets. In the roof's far corner, past a stack of firewood, you spot a squat wash-house door, small, almost hidden. Its bar is lifted off its brackets and leans against the wall. Nobody has noticed. Tessa left it open weeks ago for exactly this night, and nobody has thought to look.

At the ledger-house door you plant your heels, and the grey cloaks half-drag you before you stop them. You say it flat and loud for the room inside. You'll hear his terms, but you see Tessa alive and whole before you say a word.

The sergeant raps. A soft voice answers, and the door opens.

The room is the same room. The scorch mark runs across the floor, the table has been righted, and the stove ticks in the corner. Tessa sits beside it on a stool with a curved needle in her fingers, stitching the Foreman's side. Her wrists are bound in front of her, with a grey cloak at her shoulder. She looks up when you come in, and a dark bruise runs from her temple to her jaw. Her eyes find yours, steady, amber and clear. *Alive*, you read. She gives one small nod, no more.

The Foreman sits upright in his chair with his apron off and his shirt opened on a bare bandaged flank. The scorched ledger lies on the desk in front of him, the blackened cover closed. Beside it is a new iron-banded chest, its lid open. His brass beads are on the blotter, and the pen lies across the contract.

You ask your questions, one after another. How long will she stay? Who tends the captain's wounds? What does the count stand at tonight, and what is the fine for a hand who bleeds on the Foreman's floor? The Foreman answers some of them in his gentle voice. He lets you see her breathe, and he lets you hear that Gorrak lives. You can feel it is not enough to carry an hour, and he can feel it too.

He lays one finger on the lamp. "I will give you till this burns to the mark," he says, and the mark is a thumb's width down the glass. "Perhaps an hour. Then you will swear, Emberhide, and I will not read you the contract twice."

Dawn is about three hours off. The bell that changes the stair guard will ring then. You have one hit point, a stalled sentence in your mouth and your sister three paces away with a needle in her hand. Six grey cloaks stand around the room, and the wash-house door is on the roof outside, unbarred.

While Korvash stalled him with questions, she secretly dosed the Foreman's wine cup with poppy from her mender's kit and signalled Korvash with the clan sign for 'wait' (palm flat). entries.text:
You drag your feet up the stair and try to read the walk as you go. It's a poor night for it. The cloud sits on the gate-top like a lid, the torches gutter in the wind, and the cloaks crowd close enough to block every sightline. You come away with a muddle of shoulders and spear-points and no count you could swear to.

At the ledger-house door you plant your heels, and the guards drag you a step and stop. You say it flatly, loud enough to carry through the planks: you will hear the Foreman's terms, but you will see Tessa alive and whole with your own eyes before you say a word.

A pause. Then the Foreman's small gentle voice from inside. "Let him in. I am not a man who refuses a reasonable thing."

The room is as you left it, with the table righted and the scorch on the floor. The ledger sits on a stand beside the desk, its cover blackened, the sheaf of pages swollen at one corner where the fire bit. Two grey cloaks stand over it. The Foreman is propped in his chair under a blanket with his apron off and his torso bound in clean linen. His face is the colour of tallow, and the beads lie quiet in his lap. Tessa kneels beside him with a needle and a pot of salve, her hands steady and her face composed. She looks up when you enter. She is bruised along the jaw, and she is alive, and she is whole. She looks at your wrists, then at your face, and gives the smallest nod.

"You see," the Foreman says. "Alive and whole. Now, Emberhide, ask what you will. I have time, and I find I enjoy a man who asks questions."

So you ask, and he answers. You keep the talk moving, on the old chests and the old ledgers, on who first sold a child for a number and why the number never ends. He answers in a patient, tidy voice, now and again sipping from the cup at his elbow, which Tessa refills each time with a quiet word about the blood he's lost. The hours go by in small coin: the stove ticks, the cloaks shift their feet, the wind on the shutters drops and rises. Once, while she stitches, Tessa's free hand rests flat on her knee, palm down, the clan's *wait*. You give no sign that you have seen.

It is a little after five in the morning, and the grey has begun at the shutter-cracks. The Foreman's sentences have grown slower. His eyelids droop between words. The wine cup tilts in his hand, and one of the grey cloaks steps forward and takes it from him, sniffing it. He frowns, but only at the dregs, and sets it down. The Foreman blinks at you slowly. "You were saying," he murmurs, "about the first number."

Six grey cloaks stand in the room, and a seventh is by the door. The dawn bell will ring within the hour, and the stair guard will change. Tessa has not looked up from her stitching. Your wrists are in iron and you are at 1 hit point.

I let them walk me up, dragging my feet, and read the terrain as I go: how many cloaks, where the windows are, which door the bar sits on. At the ledger-house door I plant my heels and say in a flat voice, loud enough to carry inside, "Tell your Foreman I'll hear his terms, but I see Tessa alive and whole with my own eyes before I say a word."

Once inside, I keep my chin up and my eyes on my sister and the ledger, and I stall him with questions until the dawn bell.

You drag your feet and keep your eyes open. You get the shape of it, if not the grain. Six grey cloaks around you and two more at the ledger-house door. The gate-top walk is narrow, with a low parapet on the outer side and a drop to the scree beyond it. The window shutters are barred from within. The wash-house roof sags at the far end of the walk, and a thin line of lamplight shows under the door ahead. You can't tell how many are inside.

At the door you plant your heels and say it flat and loud, so it carries through the planks: you'll hear his terms, but you see Tessa alive and whole with your own eyes before you say a word.

The door opens before the sergeant can knock. The Foreman himself stands in it, lamp in hand, with fresh linen over his ribs and the brass beads wound tight around his fingers. He looks a good deal older than he did five hours ago, and he doesn't smile.

"You will see her," he says, in his small gentle voice. "I do not break my own bargains, Emberhide, only yours." He steps aside.

The long room has been cleaned. The table is righted, the ink is dry on a fresh sheet, and the scorched ledger lies on the desk with its cover black and its spine cracked. Tessa sits on a stool beside the cold stove with her hands bound in her lap, a clean bandage round her head, and a guard at her back with a knife held low where you can see it. Her eyes are open. They find you at once, and her chin lifts.

You open your mouth to ask your questions, and the Foreman's patience cuts you off like a blade. "I know what you are doing," he says. "You are counting hours. Three until the bell, and you would like me to fill every one with talk. I have sat through a good many men playing for time, and I find them all alike." He sets the lamp on the desk. "You have seen her. Now you will swear. The terms stand as I read them, with your sister kept here as mender. Say it, or my man behind her does what he has been told to do with the knife."

The room is very quiet. The guard behind Tessa has not moved, but the blade is a hand from her throat. Six grey cloaks stand in the doorway behind you, and the contract and the pen are waiting on the desk. You are at 1 hit point.

What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 23 ~5 PM: the freed column from Greyshaft arrived here. Aunt Veshra, the drover Hale Orrin and a crowd of Harrowmere folk, with Ushk and his ten spears who had escorted the first children home, waited at the stones. Korvash left Gorrak and the Tally-sworn here under his eye while he went in with the freed children, Tessa and Pip.

entries.text:
You lean toward Gorrak and put it plainly: Hale Orrin knows what the high road needs better than anyone, and you'll bring him and Aunt Veshra to the Stones so the captain can ask for honest pay in his own voice. Gorrak grunts, which is not a yes but is not a no. Then you stand, stretch your shoulders, and wedge yourself in beside Tessa. She mutters something in her sleep about the seventh goat and shoves her cold feet against your shin. Pip is a small lump on her other side. The fire burns down. You sleep.

The next day is a long one. The column leaves the hollow with the grey light, comes down out of the rocks, and the land opens. Frosted pasture, dry stone walls, a shepherd's hut with its door hanging open. At a ford the children stop to wash and gape at a flock of ordinary sheep. Some of the older miners cry. No one hurries them.

Near five in the afternoon, the three weathered Border Stones rise ahead against a sky the colour of pewter. A crowd waits around them: herders in wool and sheepskin, women with shawls over their heads, a boy on a fence rail who sees you first and begins to shout. Ushk and his ten spears stand off to one side, helms off, as you told them to. And at the front of the crowd, her hands folded under her shawl, stands a small, square dragonborn woman with scales faded to the colour of old brick. She doesn't wave. She just looks at Tessa, then at you, then at Tessa again, and her whole face comes apart.

Beside her, a lean weathered man with a drover's staff and a grey braid, who must be Hale Orrin, is staring up the road at forty hobgoblin spears and ninety freed hands, and doesn't yet know what he is seeing.

Behind you Dreg's column has halted at a hundred paces, as you told them. Gorrak stands at its head, bare-faced, with his hands empty. Pip has gone very still against Tessa's side.

You are at the Border Stones, with the town in front of you and the Tallies behind. What does Korvash do?

input.add_to_description: Day 23 ~5 PM: the freed column from Greyshaft reached the stones. Aunt Veshra and Hale Orrin waited there with townsfolk, warned by Ushk's earlier return. The Tally-sworn halted at the stones, helms off, spears sheathed, as Korvash promised.

entries.text:
You tell Gorrak that Hale Orrin is a drover who knows what the high road needs, and that he can ask for honest pay there in his own voice. Then you stretch your sore shoulders and settle beside your sister. "Budge up, Tess. Make room for a big brother." She grumbles in Draconic and doesn't budge an inch, so you lie down in the cold anyway, with Pip's feet in your ribs. You are asleep before the fire has burned low.

The next day is long and grey, and the column walks it. The ore road flattens into the lowland high road, and the first stubble fields appear, then the first drystone walls. By the afternoon the children have gone quiet and then loud. Ninna's friends point at hillsides they know. A girl starts to run and is called back, and runs anyway. Nobody stops her.

You reach the Border Stones a little before five, as the light goes copper. The three weathered stones stand on the rise as they always have, and there is a crowd beneath them. Herders in wool, a few townsfolk, shopkeepers with lanterns not yet lit. Ushk's ten spears stand at the back, helms off. They have kept their word too.

At the front stand Aunt Veshra, small and square in her grey shawl, and beside her a lean weathered drover with a crooked staff, who must be Hale Orrin. Pell stands between them, and a small girl with a blanket round her shoulders holds his hand. She sees you and shouts your name.

Behind you the column slows and stops. Dreg's forty spears halt at the foot of the rise. Gorrak walks up beside you, burned face bare, with his helm in his hand. The crowd goes absolutely silent.

Veshra's eyes find Tessa first. She puts her hand over her mouth.

It's nearly five in the evening. The children are home, your sister is at your side, and the whole town is watching. What does Korvash do?

The children begin to run ahead, then come back, then run ahead again. By the last hours of the afternoon they have stopped counting heads and are simply walking.

At about five, with the light going copper over the lowlands, you come over the last rise and see the three Border Stones against the sky, and below them the roofs and chimneys of Harrowmere, small and warm.

There are lanterns at the Stones. A crowd of townsfolk stands there, herders and drovers and women with shawls over their heads, forty or fifty of them. Ushk's returned children must have told them everything. At the front stands a broad old woman with iron-grey braids and a cloak the colour of dried blood, her hands folded in front of her. Beside her is a lean, weathered drover with a crook. The old woman has been looking up the road for a long time, and she knows your walk from half a mile away.

"That's Aunt Veshra," Tessa whispers. Her hand finds yours and grips it hard. Pip presses against her hip. Behind you the column has slowed. The Tally spears have fallen back, helms off as you asked, and they stand in a ragged line under the first stone. Gorrak is among them, bareheaded, with his burned face to the lanterns.

You are at full strength, with your sister's hand in yours and your aunt a hundred paces off. What does Korvash do?

line:
"Then that's the thing to put to Harrowmere, Captain," I say, leaning in. "Hale Orrin's a drover, and he'll know better than anyone what the high road needs, so I'll bring you to him and Aunt Veshra at the Stones, and let you ask for honest pay in your own voice."

I stand, stretch my sore shoulders, and add, "Tonight, though, we sleep. Tessa, budge up, and make room by the fire for a big brother."

entries.text:
Gorrak says nothing for a moment. Then he gives one short nod, the kind a captain gives a sentry who has reported correctly. "At the Stones, then. In my own voice." It seems to cost him something to say it, and he looks lighter for having said it.

You stand, stretch your sore shoulders, and go around the fire. Tessa shifts without opening her eyes and makes room, muttering that you snore like a landslide. You lie down beside her with the axe at your hand and Pip's small back against your arm. For the first time since the pass, nobody is counting you.

The night passes quietly. Dreg's sentries change twice, and a wind comes down off the mountain and smells of snow. Once you wake to find Tessa awake too, looking at the stars over the lip of the hollow and humming under her breath. She stops when she sees you looking and says only, "I keep thinking someone will come and take it back." You tell her no one will. She isn't sure she believes it yet, but she sleeps again.

Dawn comes grey and cold, a little before six on Day 23. The camp stirs. Dreg's sergeants walk the rows rousing the freed hands, and the smell of woodsmoke and thin porridge drifts through the hollow. Ahead lies the last stretch of the ore road down to the lowlands, and by dusk, the Border Stones. Beyond them, Harrowmere and Aunt Veshra's table.

You are rested and unhurt. What does Korvash do?
